newsitem.title: QATAR: Gulf states set up panel to complete tariff unity.
newsitem.headline: Gulf states set up panel to complete tariff unity.

text.p: Gulf Cooperation Council finance ministers agreed on Sunday to set up a committee to help them achieve unified tariffs -- an issue blocked by disagreement between member states almost since the birth of the alliance in 1981.

The committee should recommend a solution for disputes over 90 commodities before the political and economic bloc could forge a common customs union and set up a common market, an official statement said at the end of a two-day meeting in Doha.
Ministers from Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Bahrain, Oman, the United Arab Emirates and Kuwait attended the talks.
"The ministers decided to form a technical committee to continue efforts aimed at completing the classification of all imported products," it said.
The committee should submit its report in three months -- before ministers meet on October 18 to consider recommendations.
"The commodities on which the differences persist are mainly petrochemical products whose share in the total value of GCC imports does not exceed 3-5 percent", one official said.

GCC states have classified more than 1,000 imported goods into three categories -- those exempted from tariffs such as food and medicine, basic commodities with a tariff such as industrial goods and other goods requiring a special tax to protect domestic industries.
"Agreement on most items has been reached and we hope to reach a decision on the rest before the end of the year", Sheikh Hamad bin Faisal al-Thani, Qatar's customs director, said.
Standard customs tariffs among GCC states range from four to 12 percent, with special tariffs for some industries.
UAE's Minister of State for Finance and Industrial Affairs Mohammad Khalfan bin Kharbashi told reporters the GCC was aiming to "standardise the tariff at eight percent".
A GCC summit in December agreed to end the classification before the next summit in Kuwait, slated for December 1997.
The tariffs issue is a hurdle in the way of a free trade deal with the European Union which could open lucrative European markets to cheap petrochemicals and other goods from the Gulf.
GCC and EU foreign ministers agreed in April to set a deadline of no more than two years for completing a free trade accord - an issue under discussion for more than 10 years.

Unification of regional tariffs is also a prerequisite to a GCC common market, stipulated by a 1983 economic agreement, which also calls for the link-up of stock markets, removal of customs barriers and aligning of national currencies by 1999.
